lines.text: Five weeks ago something came up the old water tunnels under the Ward. Three days later the city council built a wall around it.
On the first night you went down the storm drain after a neighbour's dog, and walked back up with the dog under one arm and a demon behind you, doing as it was told. Nobody else has managed that.

lines.speaker: Bel
lines.text: Morning, love. Don't touch the kettle.

lines.speaker: Kettle
lines.text: Good morning! Do touch the kettle. Gently. Round the spout. Then buy the kettle, and carry it far, far away from this woman.

lines.speaker: Bel
lines.text: Bought it off a scrap cart for forty. It talks, it does tricks, and it's paid for itself twice. Don't let it sweet-talk you.

lines.speaker: Bel
lines.text: Half the Ward's been asking for you. Ines at the Lock House, Teo at the Pumphouse, Dario down by the wall. Everybody's got a plan, and every plan needs the man the demons listen to.
The kettle on Bel's counter is copper, dented, and has a striped tail it keeps trying to tuck underneath itself.

lines.speaker: Kettle
lines.text: Psst. You. The famous one. I'm not really a kettle. Well, I am now. Long story, short ending: I got stuck.

lines.speaker: Kettle
lines.text: She polishes me twice a day and charges a coin a look. Get me out of here and I'll be the best demon you ever walked off with. Mostly.
The kettle is back on Bel's counter, with a new dent, a strand of canal weed round the spout and a card tied to its tail: FOR SALE AGAIN. 60.

lines.speaker: Bel
lines.text: Fished him out of the drain grating this morning. The price went up. Dents are character.

lines.speaker: Kettle
lines.text: Don't. Don't say anything. I got as far as the canal and a duck sat on me. ...Take me with you this time? I'll be good. Mostly.

lines.speaker: Bel
lines.text: Salves, tonics, coats. Prices went up when the wall did. Take it up with the council.

lines.speaker: Bel
lines.text: I sell to the Lock House, the Pumphouse and the Wall Crew alike. I don't take sides. Somebody has to still be open when it's over.

lines.speaker: Bel
lines.text: Free advice, since you're a regular: don't promise everybody. People in a flood remember who promised them a boat.

lines.speaker: Bel
lines.text: Dario was in this morning. Bought nothing, as usual. Asked if I'd heard anything from outside, as if he isn't the one with the radio.

lines.speaker: Bel
lines.text: Funny thing. He bought valves off me to fix that radio, week one. Never came back for them. They're still in the drawer. Not that it's any of my business.

choices.text: So the radio's been dead since week one.

lines.speaker: Bel
lines.text: I never said that, love. I said I've got valves in a drawer. Are you buying something or not?

lines.speaker: Bel
lines.text: That's my boy. You'll make a shopkeeper yet.
There's a wet ring on Bel's counter where the kettle used to sit. She's polishing it anyway.

lines.speaker: Bel
lines.text: You knocked my kettle flat, love, and it rolled off down the canal, lid and all. Forty I paid for that. Forty.

lines.speaker: Bel
lines.text: Off down the canal, tail and all, and not so much as a thank-you. Forty I paid for that, love. Forty.

lines.speaker: Bel
lines.text: He'll be back. Anything that fond of money comes home when it runs out. And when he does, he's back on the counter, and you're paying for the look.

lines.speaker: Bel
lines.text: Sorry doesn't polish copper, love. Buy something.

lines.speaker: Bel
lines.text: Everybody in this Ward wants out, love. The rest of them aren't earning me a coin a look.
Ines Haldane kept the Ward's flood locks for thirty years. She still wears the keys on her belt, and people still come to her when the water does something it shouldn't.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: You came here first, lad. Before the Pumphouse, before the wall. I'll remember that.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: You've been listening to Dario. I can tell. He's a good boy with a bad plan.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: The council's terms are on the wall for anyone to read. Close the tunnels and they open the Ward. So we close the tunnels.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: There are blasting charges in the drain shed, from when the locks were built. Set them at the source and bring the roof down on it. The river was buried once. It can stay buried.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: And nobody's down there, before you go getting heroic. My Pell got out before the wall went up. He's outside, waiting for the rest of us.

choices.record: You promised Ines you would seal the source.

choices.text: And the Chapel Well? It's fed from down there.

choices.record: You wouldn't promise Ines anything yet.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: It is. The well goes when the source goes. Nobody else will tell you that, so I will.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: So we drink council water like the rest of the city, at council prices. I've paid worse for less.

choices.text: Then I'll help you seal it.
choices.record: You promised Ines you would seal the source, knowing it kills the Chapel Well.
You heard what sealing costs the Chapel Well, and wouldn't promise Ines anything.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: Good. When you're ready to go down, the charges are in the drain shed, and so am I. Don't make me come looking.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: Think, then. The water won't wait while you do.
Ines has her wrist strapped to a bit of board. She doesn't get up.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: Don't. I know you're sorry. Sorry doesn't set a bone.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: Pell would have stepped in. He always stepped in. Look where that got him.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: You gave him my charges. Thirty years I kept the water off this street, and you handed a boy a match.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: Say what you came to say. Then go and buy your salves from Bel.
Ines is on the Lock House step. She doesn't get up, and there's no second bowl.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: Dario's crew are telling the whole street you gave him my bag in a hole in the ground, where I couldn't see you do it.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: I'd rather you'd done it at the shed, lad. Then at least I'd have known who I was feeding.
Ines is on the Lock House step, trimming a lamp wick that doesn't need trimming.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: Dario's half went into the wall, and the wall's still there. I could have told him. I did tell him.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: And now he has your half as well. That's a wall coming down, and me with an empty shed. I can count, lad.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: One charge does nothing on its own, lad. Neither do I. Bring me the other half of an idea and we'll talk.
Ines is on the Lock House step with two bowls of soup, as if she knew you'd be up today. She puts one in your hands before you've said a word.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: Still carrying my bag. Good. Don't sit on it.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: Pumphouse lit up like a wedding last night. Teo's telling the street he's got a friend below now. I hope he meant one of those things of yours, lad.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: And somebody's painted LIAR over Teo's door. I'd have used smaller letters. He'd only have come closer to read them.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: Sump Row's sleeping on Chapel Hill tonight. Somebody frightened them up there. Good. Frightened is dry.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: Nothing down there but water and those things, is there. Nobody worth going heroic for.

choices.text: Pell's alive. He's down there with me.
choices.record: You told Ines her son is alive below, and that she lied to you about him.

choices.text: Something's knocking in the cistern. Three at a time.
choices.record: You told Ines something was knocking in the cistern. She said it was the pipes.
You ate Ines's soup and let her say nobody was down there.

lines.text: She sets her bowl down on the step very carefully, as if it might go off. Her face doesn't move. Her eyes don't stop.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: Is he hurt? ...No. Don't tell me. Bring him up and let me see for myself.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: I told them he got out. I needed that roof down, lad, and I couldn't have it come down on him. When the gate goes, the lower lock stays open till you're both up. That's the job now.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: Pipes knock, lad. Old iron does that.
She doesn't ask which pipe, or where. Her spoon has stopped halfway to her mouth, and it stays there until you look away.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: When the gate goes I shut the lower lock behind you. Nobody's down there. I'd know.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: Good. When the gate goes, I shut the lower lock behind you, and whatever's left down there stays down there.
She says it the way she says everything. Somewhere under her feet, Pell is waiting for you on his broom-handle splint.
She says it the way she says everything, and eats her soup, and doesn't once look at the drain.
Pell is asleep on the Lock House settle with his splint up on a cushion. Ines doesn't take her eyes off him.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: You watched me go down on the cobbles, lad, and then you went and found my boy. I've stopped trying to make those two add up.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: You gave Dario my charges, and then you sent me my son. I've been sat here an hour trying to make those two add up.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: Half a bridge, you gave me at that shed. And then the whole of my son.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: You carried my charges down there and found my boy on the way. I'd call that a fair day's work, if I were the sort to say so.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: Half the street's been through that door today. Every one of them says the same thing: we thought he was outside, Ines. As if it was their mistake.

choices.text: It wasn't theirs. You told me nobody was down there.
choices.record: You told Ines to her face that she lied to you about Pell.

choices.text: Say nothing. Sit with her a while.
choices.record: You sat with Ines and let her son's homecoming be enough.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: No. It was mine. I needed that roof down, lad, and I couldn't have it come down on him. So he had to be outside.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: If you'd believed me all the way to the bottom, I'd have buried my own son and thanked you for the job.
She says it flat, the way she says everything. Then she gets up and stirs the soup, because her hands need something to do.
After a while she gets up and puts a bowl of soup in your hands without a word. It's very good soup.
The Pumphouse hums. Teo Marchetti has the only electric light this side of the canal, and he sells it by the hour.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: There he is. The man the demons follow home. Sit, sit. You look like you haven't had a hot drink since the wall went up.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: And you came to me first. Before the Lock House, before the wall. I'm touched, beautiful. I'm also not surprised.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: Ines sent you? No. Ines doesn't send anyone anywhere. She stands in a doorway being right until you leave.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: You know how this started? The Undergate gave. Old iron, friend, ninety years of it. Nobody's fault. But a broken gate's an opportunity, if you're the sort of man who looks.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: Here's my pitch. There's a god at the bottom of the river, strong enough to turn every turbine I've got. This ledger's a contract. He signs, and the Ward has light, clean water and work for good. We never need the council again.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: Small print: nobody signs standing up. You'd have to put him on his back first. I've seen how you work. You could.

choices.record: You took Teo's ledger and promised to bind the god for him.

choices.text: A god in harness? That never ends well.
choices.record: You told Teo a god in harness never ends well.
You wouldn't take Teo's ledger yet.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: Beautiful. Bring it back signed and you'll never pay for a bulb again. I'll put that in writing. I put everything in writing.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: Everything's in harness, friend. That river was in harness under your floorboards for ninety years, and nobody minded till it got out.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: Not yet is my favourite kind of no. The door's open, and so's the kettle.
Teo has a hot cup in your hands before you're through the Pumphouse door. The turbine's hum comes through the wall like a held breath.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: You've been all the way down, haven't you? Turbine hall and everything. You've got the look. Beautiful old wheel. Ninety years and she still turns.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: And every bulb I own doubled last night. That was you, wasn't it? The intake. I could kiss you. I might, if you stand still.

choices.record: You held Teo's own wrench up in front of him.

choices.text: There's a wrench under that winch with your name stamped on it.
choices.record: You told Teo you'd seen his wrench jammed in the winch.

choices.text: Beautiful wheel. *Drink your tea and say nothing.*
choices.record: You drank Teo's tea and said nothing about the gate.

lines.text: He reads his own name on the handle the way a man reads his handwriting on a note he never meant to leave. He doesn't reach for it.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: You already had it out of me over the counter. Saying it twice doesn't make it lighter.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: Old iron. Five weeks I've been saying old iron. You'd think by now I'd believe it.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: Yes. I wedged it. I wanted this Ward to have lights. I didn't know what was behind the gate. Nobody did.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: And Pell saw me do it. He went down to undo it, and I let everyone go on believing he'd got out.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: Tell them, and they'll hang me off the Drain Bridge and the lights go out with me. Or keep it between us, and I'll owe you. I always pay what I owe.

choices.record: You told the Ward that Teo wedged the gate open.
You kept Teo's secret, and made him owe you for it.
You left Teo waiting to find out whether you'll tell.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: Ninety years of iron, friend. Nobody's fault.
He tops up your cup, and watches you drink every drop of it.
By dark the whole Ward knows. Somebody paints LIAR over POWER BY THE HOUR in letters a foot high. Nobody stops buying the light.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: See? They hate me and they still want the lights on. That's the Ward. That's everyone.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: I always pay. Ask anyone. ...Actually, don't ask anyone.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: Take your time, friend. I'll be here, keeping the lights on for everyone you haven't told.
Down by the wall, Dario Venn and his crew have been chipping at the concrete for a week, right where the old culvert runs under it. Somebody has painted WE LIVE HERE across the blocks.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: Me first? Before Ines and her soup, before Teo and his lights? ...Don't say anything. I want to enjoy it.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: You've been to the Lock House. You smell like her soup.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: And Teo's had his hand on your shoulder. Count your fingers.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: Everyone wants to fix the tunnels. Forget the tunnels. The Ward isn't the streets, it's us. Get us out and let the city deal with its own buried river.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: Ines has two blasting charges in the drain shed. Put them under this culvert and the wall comes down. We walk out in daylight, all of us, together.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: My sister's on the other side. She's got rooms lined up, work, all of it. I talk to her on the radio every night. It's all arranged.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: ...You're staring. Sorry. You've got a face people stare at. That's not a line. Well. It's a bit of a line.

choices.text: I'm with you. Let's get everyone out.
choices.record: You promised Dario you would get everyone out.

choices.text: And everything in the tunnels walks out with us?
choices.record: You asked Dario whether the demons walk out too.
You flirted back at Dario.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: Yeah? Yeah. Right. Don't look at me for a second, I'm doing something stupid with my face.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: If it walks behind you, it can walk behind us. I'm not leaving anyone behind, mate. Not even the ugly ones.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: There wasn't a rest of it. I had one line and I used it on a man who walks into sewers for fun.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: Get us out of here and I'll write a better one. That's a promise. You don't have to make one back.
'Is she all right? Ines? I never meant for her to...' Dario can't finish it, and he can't quite look at you either.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: Half a door. I'm still working out whether that was clever or cruel.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: You backed me. In front of Ines, in front of everyone. I'm not going to forget that.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: You picked her. I know. And I'm still talking to you, so that tells you what kind of idiot I am.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: Mind yourself down there. I mean it.
The Wall Crew's radio sits in its crate at the foot of the wall, headphones hung on a nail.
Dario is chalking a new line on the radio log: DAY 33. SHE SAYS SOON. He finishes the last letter before he looks round.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: She was on last night. Asked after everyone. There's a room with a window for whoever gets through first.

choices.text: Bel still has the valves you bought for that radio. It's been dead since week one.
choices.record: You told Dario you knew his radio had been dead since the first week.
You let Dario go on chalking messages from a dead radio.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: ...Course you know. Somebody saw me put my boot through it.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: You've already made me say it once. Don't make me say it twice.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: There's no message. There hasn't been one since the first week. I don't even know if she's alive.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: But if I tell them nobody's waiting, they won't walk. And if they don't walk, they'll drown in here waiting for the council to remember them.

choices.text: Tell them the truth. Let them choose.
choices.record: You made Dario tell his crew that nobody is waiting outside.

choices.text: Keep telling it. They need somewhere to walk to.
choices.record: You told Dario to keep lying to his crew about his sister.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: A room with a window. Imagine that.
He pockets the chalk and straightens the headphones on their nail, as if somebody might be about to call.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: ...Yeah. Okay. Stand next to me while I tell them? Not close. Just there.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: Somewhere to walk to. Right. ...Don't tell me I'm a good liar. I know I am.
The drain shed is open. Dario's crew has it surrounded, and Ines is standing in the doorway with an oilcloth bag of charges held against her chest like a cat that wants to bite.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: Two charges. That wall's been standing on our necks for five weeks. Ines, please. Give them here.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: They go to the source, Dario. You blow that wall and the council puts up a bigger one, with guns on it.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: You told me you'd seal it, lad. Here's where you show me.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: You said you were with us. You said it to my face.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: Then he decides. He's the one going down. Go on. Tell her.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: Yes. Tell me.

choices.text: Ines is right. They go to the source.
choices.record: You backed Ines at the drain shed and took both charges.
You backed Dario at the drain shed and made Ines hand him both charges.
You split the charges at the drain shed: one for Dario, one for you.
You walked past the drain shed and let them fight it out. Ines went down.

lines.text: Ines puts the bag in your hands without a word. It's heavier than it looks.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: Right. Right. Remember this when the water's at your chin.
He leaves the yard without looking back. His crew follows him. One of them is crying.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: He'll forgive you or he won't. The source, lad. Nowhere else.
Ines looks at you for a long moment. Then she holds the bag out to Dario at arm's length, like something dead.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: Thirty years I kept the water off this Ward. You'll see what he does with those, and you'll remember who handed them over.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: We won't waste them. I swear. One to test the wall, one for the day. You'll hear it.
He squeezes your shoulder on the way past, hard, as if he's checking you're real.
Nobody likes it. Ines hands one charge to Dario as if it were her own tooth. The other she pushes into your hands.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: One charge won't bring down the source. You know that.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: And one won't bring down the wall. Thanks. Really. Half a door.
They walk off in opposite directions, and both of them look back at you the same way: as if you'd handed them half a bridge.
You step past them, towards the drain. Behind you it stops being an argument.
Someone shoves. Ines goes down hard on the cobbles. The bag splits: one charge rolls into the canal with a fat splash, and Dario's crew are gone with the other before she's up.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: You stood there. You stood there and watched.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: *from the bridge* I didn't mean for her to fall! Ines! I didn't mean it!
The Ward smells of cordite. Down by the wall a yard of concrete is gone from the base of the barrier, and the gap is full of council floodlights.
A loudspeaker on the far side repeats itself every minute: ANY FURTHER DAMAGE TO THE BOUNDARY WILL BE MET WITH FORCE.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: It cracked and it held. One more and it goes, I swear it. They can't shoot all of us.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: That was the only one we had. It cracked and it held, and now they've got lights on us all night.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: Now they'll never open it. Are you happy?

choices.text: Take my charge. Make it count.
choices.record: You gave Dario your charge for the wall.
You told Dario to keep his crew's heads down.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: Two's enough. You hear that, wall? ...Sorry. I talk to it now.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: Heads down is how they walled us in in the first place. ...All right. For you.
Pell got up the drain ahead of you on his broom-handle splint, and the Ward found out in about four minutes. Half of it is in the street.
Behind him Sump Row is emptying. He knocked on every door on the way home, splint and all.
Ines is holding on to her son with both arms, as if the water might come back up the drain for him.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: I told them you were outside. I told myself. If you were outside, nobody had to go down after you and drown.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: Thank you. And now there's nobody down there, I can bring the roof down on it with a clear conscience.

lines.speaker: Pell
lines.text: Mum. Not now. Not today.

lines.speaker: Ines
lines.text: Lad. ...There's soup. There's always soup.
A kodama comes pattering down the passage behind you with a dented soup tin held over its head like a crown. It sets the tin at your feet, bows, and waits.
A note is tied to the handle in a square lock-keeper's hand: HE'S HOME. LEG'S SET. HE SAYS THE LITTLE ONES FED HIM, SO I'M FEEDING YOU.
Under that: HE KNOCKED ON EVERY DOOR IN SUMP ROW ON THE WAY. THEY'RE ALL UP THE HILL.
And at the bottom, smaller, pressed hard into the paper: I TOLD EVERYONE HE GOT OUT. YOU KNEW BETTER. THANK YOU, LAD. — I.H.

lines.speaker: Kodama
lines.text: ...thank you, lad... ...lad... *it rattles its head like dry seeds, picks up the empty tin and patters back up the tunnel*
Coming up out of the drain you can see the whole of Sump Row: the low street, the washing lines, a man sweeping his step, two kids racing paper boats in the puddles.
The survey was very clear. If the river comes back, it comes back through those front doors first.

choices.text: Go door to door. Get them up the hill tonight.
choices.record: You went door to door and got Sump Row up Chapel Hill.

choices.text: Say nothing. No sense frightening them over an old drawing.
choices.record: You looked at Sump Row and said nothing.

lines.text: It takes two hours and every front door. Dario's crew carries mattresses up Chapel Hill. Nobody quite believes you, and everybody goes anyway.
Half the Pumphouse shift lives on Sump Row. Teo stands in his doorway and watches them walk off the job to pack.
A kid sails a paper boat past your boots and down the drain grating. It doesn't come back up.
The culverts smell of wet brick and something older. Water moves somewhere ahead, louder than it should.
Chalk on the wall at head height, in a hand you don't know: an arrow, the word HOME, and the arrow points down.
A little man in a leather apron is sitting on an upturned bucket, hammering a tiny shoe, with his back to a heap of coins he is very obviously not guarding.

lines.speaker: Leprechaun
lines.text: Gold? What gold? Would ye look at that, behind you! ...No? Ah, well.
In a brick chamber off the culvert someone has scrubbed the moss off a carved stone as tall as a man. Hester Quill is sitting in front of it with a torch, a flask and a notebook.

lines.speaker: Hester
lines.text: Oh, thank goodness, a person. Look. SALLOW. They carved the river's name here before they bricked it over. Ninety years in the dark, and somebody still bothered to write it down.

lines.speaker: Hester
lines.text: Everyone up there talks about the demons like a leak. They're not a leak. They're what lived in the river, coming home. You don't stop a river coming home. You get out of its way.

lines.speaker: Hester
lines.text: All she wants is her old bed back, and her bed is under the empty streets at the bottom of the Ward. Hardly anyone lives down there now.

lines.speaker: Hester
lines.text: Take this. It's the boundary marker they pulled up when they built the culverts. If you reach whatever's at the source, show it that someone up here remembers its name.

choices.record: You promised Hester you would speak for the river, and took her Sallow Stone.

choices.text: Out of its way? People live in its way.
choices.record: You told Hester that people live in the river's way.

choices.text: You came down here alone? Are you all right?

lines.speaker: Hester
lines.text: Bless you. I'm fifty-one, I have a flask, and the little tree spirits keep bringing me mushrooms. I'm better than I've been in years.

lines.speaker: Hester
lines.text: Will you take the stone? Will you speak for her?

choices.record: You promised Hester you would speak for the river, and took her Sallow Stone.
You wouldn't promise Hester anything yet.

lines.speaker: Hester
lines.text: Oh, my dear. She'll be so pleased. Well. I will be. I'm told rivers don't do pleased.

lines.speaker: Hester
lines.text: Hardly anyone, my dear. I've been through the maps. Well. Some of the maps.

lines.speaker: Hester
lines.text: Quite right. Never promise a river anything you haven't read up on.

lines.speaker: Hester
lines.text: You look like a man carrying bad news down a corridor.

lines.speaker: Hester
lines.text: Sump Row? No. No, the survey must be... Sump Row is two hundred people. Mrs. Adeyemi. The Kowalski boys. I teach half those children.

lines.speaker: Hester
lines.text: I said nobody lives there. I believed it. I never once walked down that street and counted.

choices.text: You know every family. Go up and get them out.
choices.record: You sent Hester up to get Sump Row out.

choices.text: Then we get them out first. Then the river.
choices.record: You told Hester: people out first, then the river.

choices.text: Then maybe the river can't come home.
choices.record: You told Hester the river might not be able to come home.

lines.speaker: Hester
lines.text: Every family. Every name. I'll have them up Chapel Hill by dark, my dear, and I'll count them twice.
She packs her notebook and her flask and goes up the culvert at a pace that scatters the kodama.

lines.speaker: Hester
lines.text: Yes. People first, then her. She's waited ninety years. She can wait one more night.

lines.speaker: Hester
lines.text: Maybe. ...Let me sit with her a while. Go on, my dear. I'll be here.
Hester is standing in the middle of Sump Row with a clipboard, ticking off doors. Half of them stand open.

lines.speaker: Hester
lines.text: Two hundred and six. I counted twice. Mrs. Adeyemi made me count her cat.

lines.speaker: Hester
lines.text: I still want her to come home, my dear. I just want her to find the house empty when she does.
A boom rolls through the rock from somewhere above and behind you. Dust sifts down from the vault. Something in the dark goes very quiet, then starts to scream.
Dario has found a use for his charge.
Very faintly, from somewhere far above, somebody is cheering. Somebody else is shouting at them to stop.
A waterworks clerk's office, flooded once and dried out since. On the wall, under cracked glass, a survey of the Sallow Culvert, ninety years old.
The old riverbed is drawn in blue. The streets drawn over it are labelled in a neat hand: Sump Row. Sump Row. Sump Row.
If the river ever comes back, it comes back there first. Every house. Every door.
Somebody ought to tell Sump Row. The clerk who drew this certainly didn't.
Dario is in the clerk's office with a torch in his teeth, tracing the old survey with one finger. He doesn't look round.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: There's an outfall under the wall on this map. Bricked up ninety years. You wouldn't give me a way through the wall, so I'm looking for one under it.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: Look at this, though. Sump Row. The river runs right under Sump Row. If Hester gets her way, that's my street gone.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: You've still got the charges. I'm not going to ask nicely twice. ...No, I am. I'm asking nicely twice. Please.

choices.record: You gave Dario Ines's charges, below ground, behind her back.

choices.text: Sump Row's your street. Go up and get them out.
choices.record: You sent Dario up to get Sump Row out.

choices.text: Go back up. It's not safe down here.
choices.record: You sent Dario back up without the charges.
You refused Dario the charges.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: Both? You're mad. Thank you. I'm going to kiss that wall when it comes down. Then maybe you.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: My street. My nan's street. ...Right. Every door, I swear. Don't wait for me.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: Safe. Right. I'll go up. You keep going down, apparently, because you're like that.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: Don't be sorry. Be right. You'd better be right.
Dario's back at the wall, filthy to the elbows. He puts his chisel down when he sees you, which he never does.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: Every door on Sump Row, like you said. My nan wouldn't go up the hill without her budgie, so the budgie's on Chapel Hill too.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: Cost us a day at the wall, and half the crew's saying I've gone soft. You picked her, and I'm still running your errands. Tells you what kind of idiot I am.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: Ines's charges are under my bed, wrapped in my good coat. I haven't slept. She walked past the wall this morning and didn't look at me. That's worse than shouting.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: You picked her. I know. And I'm still talking to you, so that tells you what kind of idiot I am.

lines.speaker: Dario
lines.text: Mind yourself down there. I mean it.
The cistern: a lake of black water under a brick vault, so still it looks solid. Lamps someone lit weeks ago are still guttering on the walkways.
Somewhere beyond it, metal on metal: knock, knock, knock. A pause. Knock, knock, knock.
A winged hart with a tail of fire is lounging across the walkway as if it were a sofa. The sparks from his tail hiss out on the water.

lines.speaker: Furfur
lines.text: Ah! A visitor. I am the Duke of this cistern, I own every drop of it, and I am absolutely telling the truth. First question, before business, I ask everyone: top or bottom?
At the back of the gallery a man is sitting against a pump housing with one leg splinted to a broom handle, knocking on a pipe with a spanner. He stops when he sees you.

lines.speaker: Pell
lines.text: Three weeks I've been knocking on that pipe, with the water an inch from the door. You drained it. Christ.

lines.speaker: Pell
lines.text: I'm Pell. Ines's son. Let me guess what she's been telling people. That I got out.

lines.speaker: Pell
lines.text: I came down the night the gate went, to shut it, and couldn't. Don't take my word for why. Go and look at the winch in the turbine hall, next level down.

lines.speaker: Pell
lines.text: I can walk, just. I know a back way to the gate, through the old shrine on that level. Or I can go home. Your call. I'm too tired to make mine.

choices.text: Go home. Your mother needs to see you.
choices.record: You sent Pell home to his mother.

choices.text: Go home, and knock on every door in Sump Row on the way.
choices.record: You sent Pell home to knock on every door in Sump Row.

choices.text: Stay with me. Show me the back way.
choices.record: You kept Pell below to show you the back way.

lines.speaker: Pell
lines.text: Yes, boss. She's going to hit me, you know. Then she's going to make soup.
He goes off up the gallery on his broom-handle splint, knocking on the wall as he passes, for luck.

lines.speaker: Pell
lines.text: Sump Row. I grew up two doors off it. ...I'll knock on every one. I've had the practice.

lines.speaker: Pell
lines.text: Right. Mind the step on the shrine stair. I didn't, once.

lines.speaker: Pell
lines.text: One thing. When the gate goes, Mum shuts the lower lock. Always has. She only does it when she's sure the galleries are empty.
The old turbine hall. The great wheel is still turning, slowly, driven by river water forced up from the Undergate. This is where the Ward's light comes from.

The gate winch at the far wall is bent open past its stops, its gear teeth sheared clean off. Nobody is closing anything from here. On the floor under it lies a pipe wrench, and stamped into the handle: PUMPHOUSE, T. MARCHETTI.
Beside the wheel there's an intake valve, chalked in Teo's tidy hand: OPEN = A YEAR OF POWER. Under it, in someone else's: AND WHAT ELSE COMES THROUGH?

choices.record: You took Teo's stamped wrench from under the winch.

choices.text: Leave the wrench where it fell.
choices.record: You left Teo's wrench where it fell.

lines.text: It's heavier than a wrench should be. You can feel the letters with your thumb.
You leave it where it fell. Somebody ought to see it there, exactly as it is.
That leaves Teo's intake valve, and the chalk.

choices.record: You opened Teo's turbine intake.
You left Teo's turbine intake shut.

lines.text: The valve turns with a groan and the great wheel picks up speed. Far above, every bulb in the Pumphouse brightens. Something else comes in through the intake with the water, and swims off into the dark.
You leave the valve shut. The wheel turns on, slow and patient, like something that can wait.
A woman in grey is sitting on the rubble with her hair over her face, combing it with a silver comb. Her keening fills the hall and doesn't echo.

lines.speaker: Banshee
lines.text: Haldane. Haldane. I'm singing for a Haldane. One of that name is still under the stone, and the water is coming for him.

lines.speaker: Banshee
lines.text: Don't hide him behind you, a stór. The water knows where he's standing.
A woman in grey is sitting on the rubble, combing her hair with a silver comb, keening.

lines.speaker: Banshee
lines.text: Marchetti. Marchetti. I'm singing for the man who sold the light. Don't look at me like that. I don't decide. I only sing.
Here is the stone's twin, the one from the culverts, with an empty socket in its face where a marker used to sit.
Hester's Sallow Stone is exactly the right size. When you hold it up, the water around your boots goes very still, as if it's listening.

choices.text: Set the stone back in its socket.
choices.record: You set the Sallow Stone back in its socket.
You kept the Sallow Stone.

lines.text: It goes in with a sound like a held breath let out. Somewhere far below, something enormous turns its head.
The water around your boots starts moving again. It doesn't seem offended. It seems patient.
The last clean spring before the source. Overhead, through the rock, something enormous shifts its weight, and the whole tunnel answers with a long iron groan.
The Undergate won't hold much longer. Whatever is behind it knows that too.

lines.speaker: Pell
lines.text: That's the gate. That noise. It's worse than last week.
The water is cold enough to hurt your teeth. Behind the rock the groaning stops, as if something down there is listening to you drink.

A stall has been knocked together out of a boat: the hull upended on two barrels, oars for shelves, a lantern hung off the tiller. Behind it, leaning on a pole as if it were still a ferry, is a filthy old man with eyes like two fixed flames.

lines.speaker: Charon
lines.text: Fare. ...No. Habit. You drained my lake, passenger, so I don't have a ferry any more. I have a shop.

lines.speaker: Charon
lines.text: And you've sent me a lot of custom this week. Not one of them had an obol.

lines.speaker: Charon
lines.text: Salves, tonics, the green muck the kappa make. Prices are what they are; pitch doesn't grow on trees, and there are no trees. I'll hold your coat while you try another one on, too. For a fee.

The Undergate fills the end of the cavern: iron leaves taller than houses, weeping water from every rivet. In front of it something enormous is coiled, a man's face on a serpent's body, red hair drifting as if the air were river.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: So. The mud-dwellers send Us a little fish. They buried Our river under their houses, and now they wonder why the water comes looking.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: Someone set Our name back in its stone. We felt it. Was that you, little fish?

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: You killed a great many of Our river's children on the way down. We counted every one.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: You killed a great many of Our children, and let a few of them go. We counted both. We have not yet decided which one is you.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: You let Our children go when you could have killed them. They told Us. We do not forget a kindness; it happens too rarely.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: And you run, little fish. Fish do. Run now, if you like.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: The gate breaks either way. We are only deciding whether you are standing in front of it. So: what have you carried all this way?

choices.record: You showed Gonggong the Sallow Stone.
You showed Gonggong Teo's stamped wrench.

choices.text: Tell him who wedged the gate open.
choices.record: You told Gonggong who wedged the gate open.
You told Gonggong about Sump Row.

choices.text: Call the river by her name: Sallow.
choices.record: You called the river by her name to her god's face.
You showed Gonggong Teo's ledger.
You showed Gonggong the charges.
You showed Gonggong your single charge.

choices.text: Tell him he looks strong. And virile. *Wink.*
choices.record: You told a river god he looked strong and virile, and winked.
You offered a river god gold.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: What else, little fish?

choices.record: You showed Gonggong the Sallow Stone.
You showed Gonggong Teo's stamped wrench.

choices.text: Tell him who wedged the gate open.
choices.record: You told Gonggong who wedged the gate open.
You told Gonggong about Sump Row.

choices.text: Call the river by her name: Sallow.
choices.record: You called the river by her name to her god's face.
You showed Gonggong Teo's ledger.
You showed Gonggong the charges.
You showed Gonggong your single charge.

choices.text: Tell him he looks strong. And virile. *Wink.*
choices.record: You told a river god he looked strong and virile, and winked.
You offered a river god gold.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: SALLOW. Our name, in a mud-dweller's hand. They pulled that stone out of Our bank ninety years ago and used it to prop a door.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: And you carried it all the way down to show Us. Hm.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: So that is the hand that opened Our door. A merchant's. For light, by the hour.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: You bring Us the truth of it, little fish. Down here that is rarer than gold.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: A merchant, for light by the hour. We had wondered whose hand it was. You did not have to tell Us that.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: Sump Row. We know the street. It is lying in Our bed.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: And you sent them up their hill before you came down. Good. Our river does not need them drowned. Only gone.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: Two hundred of you, asleep where Our water ran. Your clerks put them there, little fish, not We. The water will not ask their names.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: ...Sallow. Few say it any more. Fewer say it to Us.
For a moment the water around your knees runs warm, and it is only a river.
The coils shift. A slow, enormous smile spreads across the man's face, and a loop of serpent slides round behind you, not quite touching.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: Bold little fish. We have been called a great many things by mud-dwellers. Not that. Not in ninety years.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: Say it again when the water is at your chin, and We will see if you mean it. It does not open the gate.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: A contract. For a god. In a merchant's tidy hand.
The water around your knees goes very cold.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: If you want Our name at the bottom of that, little fish, you will have to put Us on Our back first.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: You came to bring the roof down on Us, and you show Us the means. At least you are not a liar. Liars We drown first.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: Half a bomb. You could not even carry down enough to bury Us. We are almost touched.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: Gold. You bring a river god yellow stones. We have whole beds of them, little fish. You call them riverbeds.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: Keep them. We are not for sale, little fish, and neither is the gate.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: Then speak, or fight. The water is listening.
The iron screams. A rivet the size of a fist shoots out of the Undergate, and the first real water comes through, black and cold, around your knees.
Pell is beside you on his broom-handle splint, staring at the gate he couldn't close.

Up in the Ward they'll feel it now. Ines at her shed. Teo at the Pumphouse with his hand on the turbine levers. Dario's crew at the wall. Hester's people on the hill. Bel behind her counter, watching the door.

Ines does what a lock-keeper does when the gate goes and she is sure nobody is below: she shuts the lower lock. The backwash comes down the culvert at chest height and takes Pell off his one good leg. You get a fist in his collar. Only just.
Ines leaves the lower lock open. She knows who's down here. The backwash goes past you down the old culvert, and Pell laughs once, like a man who knows exactly why.

Ines shuts the lower lock: nobody's down there, she's told everyone. Somewhere east of the cistern, under the scream of the gate, a spanner stops knocking on a pipe. After a long moment it starts again, slower.
And on Sump Row, two hundred people are asleep on the old riverbed.
Every one of them told you where the water should go, and you said yes to more of them than the water can satisfy.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: Well, little fish? Our river is coming either way. Tell Us where it goes.

lines.speaker: Gonggong
lines.text: You have beaten Us. Enjoy it. The water does not care who won.
The gate has minutes, and you're the one standing in front of it.
Word travels fast in a walled-in Ward. By the time you're over the Drain Bridge, people are talking about you, and not quietly.
A man on the bridge nudges his friend. 'That's him. Put down a whole pile of them down there, they say. Good.'
'Talks to them,' a woman says. 'Just talks. Like they're people.'
Somebody hurries their kids indoors as your demons file past behind you.
An old woman presses a boiled sweet into your hand. 'For the ones you let go,' she says, and won't say how she knows.
'Ran from two of them, I heard,' someone says behind you. Somebody else laughs.
'Winked at one of them,' a man mending a net tells nobody in particular. 'One of the big ones. Swear it winked back.'

lines.speaker: Bel
lines.text: Still alive, love? Good. Dead men don't buy salves.
Every bulb in the Pumphouse is burning, and there's a queue round the corner for the light.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: Partner. Your name's next to every hour of that light in my book. I always pay.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: They painted LIAR on my door and then queued under it for the light you gave me. I'm not complaining. I'm counting.

lines.speaker: Teo
lines.text: A year of power, friend. Whatever else comes through that intake, we'll be able to see it coming.

lines.speaker: Hester
lines.text: You did it. You put her stone back. I felt the water change, all the way up here: it went still, and then it went warm.

lines.speaker: Hester
lines.text: She knows somebody up here remembers her name now. Whatever you decide at the gate, my dear, she knows that.
There's a clean ring on Bel's counter where the kettle used to sit.

lines.speaker: Bel
lines.text: Forty I paid for that kettle. Forty, and he never once boiled.

lines.speaker: Bel
lines.text: Keep him. Feed him. If he comes back here with a tail and a debt, I'm charging you both.
